paras: The shooting at Henry Beck's farm was the killing of five Black men and the mortal wounding of two others by Deputy Sheriff Sid Cauley of Carroll County, Mississippi, in late July or early August 1910. According to the only dispatch, from Elliott, the men attacked the deputy with axes and pitchforks when he came to arrest them, and he shot all seven in about ten seconds. The story spread as a short wire item, drew a mocking editorial in praise of Mississippi marksmanship from the Chicago Inter Ocean, and was cited by the Seattle Republican as an example of wholesale killing of Black people.

The dispatch said Cauley had gone to Henry Beck's farm to arrest a group of Black men "for an assult," without saying whom they were accused of assaulting. In this account the men attacked him with axes and pitchforks, and Cauley, using a revolver in each hand, killed five and mortally wounded two, the "battle" lasting ten seconds. None of the dead or wounded was named, and the papers do not say whether Henry Beck, the farm's owner, was among them.

The Inter Ocean's retelling added that the men "were not only resisting arrest, but were advancing on the deputy" with the "avowed intention of cutting him down." It also said they had made the sheriff "take to the woods" the day before, a detail absent from the wire brief.
No report of an inquest, an arrest or any charge against the deputy appears in the coverage, and no later report on the two mortally wounded men was found.

The white press carried the story mostly as a filler under the headline "A Sheriff's Battle With Negroes," printed verbatim in country weeklies in Missouri and Kansas between August 4 and 11. The Rich Hill Tribune ran it twice, a week apart, and the Chanute Times carried the same text. South Dakota weeklies printed a shortened version in a general-news column between items on Panama Canal excavation and a flour-company scandal.

The Chicago Inter Ocean turned the dispatch into a humorous editorial, "Quick Shooting in South," calling it a "remarkable shooting record" and arguing that Mississippi "has never got the credit it deserves as a sharpshooting State." The editorial was reprinted in the San Antonio Light and Gazette on August 8 and in the Washington Herald on August 25, the latter under the subhead "Mississippi Leads Other States in Rapid-fire Homicides."

Two Black papers took the story up in different ways. The Wichita Searchlight reprinted the white wire brief, headline and all, without comment on August 6. A day earlier the Seattle Republican, in a sarcastic front-page editorial titled "Perfect Peace Preserved," described a Mississippi deputy who found "some ten or a dozen" men talking, "declared" they planned to attack him with clubs, and shot down five "in order to show his authority." The paper paired the case with a mass killing of Black people in Texas and mocked the press's stories of Black "uprisings," adding that such tales held "if the press of the country can be relied upon."

The accounts differ on the threat the men posed: the wire and the Inter Ocean say they attacked with axes and pitchforks, while the Seattle Republican says the deputy only claimed they were planning to attack him with clubs. The wire said Cauley came to arrest several men, the Seattle Republican one man; every version rests on the deputy's side of the story, and no independent or local account was found.

reader.title: Shooting at Henry Beck's farm, Carroll County, Mississippi
bases: A deputy sheriff acting alone shot seven Black men while trying to arrest them, with no mob or posse reported (A1, A11).

Every report traces to one dispatch from Elliott, Miss., carried as a wire brief (A1, A2) and paraphrased in editorials (A4, A11); no local, inquest or independent account was found, and the Seattle Republican's version recasts the justification without denying the shooting (A4).

accounts.label: Wire report (deputy's version)
accounts.gist: The men attacked Cauley with axes and pitchforks at Henry Beck's farm when he came to arrest them for an assault; he fired a revolver in each hand, killing five and mortally wounding two in ten seconds.

accounts.label: Chicago Inter Ocean editorial
accounts.gist: The men were resisting arrest and advancing with axes and pitchforks intending to cut the deputy down, having driven the sheriff into the woods the day before.

accounts.label: Seattle Republican editorial
accounts.gist: The deputy went to arrest one man, found ten or a dozen talking together, 'declared' they were planning to attack him with clubs, and shot down five 'in order to show his authority'.

framing.detail: Country weeklies in Missouri, Kansas and South Dakota ran the brief under 'A Sheriff's Battle With Negroes', presenting the deputy's account of an armed attack as fact.
The Chicago Inter Ocean editorial, reprinted in San Antonio and Washington, called it a 'remarkable shooting record' and joked that Mississippi deserved credit 'as a sharpshooting State'.
The Seattle Republican's 'Perfect Peace Preserved' mocked the press's tales of Black 'uprisings' and cast the deputy's claim of an attack as a pretext for killing.
The Wichita Searchlight printed the white wire brief and headline unchanged, without comment.
